name: Jamal Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tired, mostly. I'm doing paramedic science, so I'm in lectures about the body and a practical on bandaging and CPR on a plastic dummy called Kevin. Four nights a week I pick orders at a warehouse out on the ring road, ten at night till six in the morning on the weekend, shorter on weeknights. Then I sleep on the bus. I live at home with my mum and my gran, in a flat where I share a room with the ironing board.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any computers or AI at the warehouse or the course?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Money. The loan pays the fees. My mum cleans offices and my gran has a small pension, so nobody has spare cash. I've got about two weeks of food money put aside. I don't talk about it much, I just do the shifts. Got in with average grades, no scholarship, so I figure I just have to work harder than the lads with better results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough. I've heard the hype for a couple of years and nothing much has changed where I work. If it's mostly hype, then it's a lot of talk about nothing. I'd tell the lads on shift it's all noise and we should just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd say good. I like things staying how they are. I don't need the world to change, I need my shifts and my degree. But I'd still be worried about money and about being wrecked from nights. That's where the stress is, not the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Do my shifts, go to lectures, read on the bus. I'd try to get a couple more day shifts at the warehouse so I'm not so knackered. I'd keep the paramedic placement and pass the first-year exams. I wouldn't change anything. If it's not broken, don't fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, I suppose. Not happy, but settled. Like I know where the walls are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the warehouse already doing with machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got scanners that tell you the shortest route round the racks and a little robot trolley on one aisle. Nobody's lost a job to it yet. The trolley breaks down more than it works. I don't use AI myself, never have. I don't trust what it says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you change the degree, even in this quiet picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Paramedic work is the one thing I actually want to do. My uncle was a paramedic. I'd change my mind only if I couldn't afford it, and in this picture I can just about manage. So the money decides, not the technology.

say: I'd tell the lads on shift it's **all noise** and we should get on with it.
I'd say nothing much has **changed** where I work.
think: I like things staying how they are: I need my **shifts** and my degree.
The stress is **money** and being wrecked from nights, not computers.
do: Keep doing **nights** at the warehouse and read on the bus.
Ask for a couple more **day shifts** so I'm less tired.
Pass the first-year **exams** and keep the paramedic placement.
feel: **Settled**, like I know where the walls are.
S0.quote: I don't need the world to change, I need my shifts and my degree.
fieldNote: Jamal wants **stability**; he is resistant to AI and distrusts what it says.
His anxiety comes from **money and exhaustion** rather than technology, even in the quiet picture.
The warehouse already has a trolley robot that mostly breaks down, which shapes his scepticism.

steps.text: Keep the warehouse night shifts and read on the bus
Ask for more day shifts at the warehouse
Pass the first-year exams before thinking about anything else

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what happens, and most people will cope. I'd tell my mates the warehouse will use more machines, but you can't automate a person carrying an old lady down the stairs. I'd say people should keep their heads down and keep learning on the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be nervous. The warehouse is the first place where it bites, because ordering and routing are the sort of thinking jobs the card talks about. If they need fewer pickers, my nights go. And I'd be left with the degree and no income to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my supervisor about moving to the stock control desk where you check deliveries. I'd stick with the paramedic degree. If they cut my hours, I'd go for agency work, the kind that pays the same but no promises. I'd stop spending on anything except food and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sick. Like when you hear there's a storm coming and you're still outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own warehouse tasks could software take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The route planning, the stock counts, and the paperwork on arrival. A computer does all that now. What it can't do yet is lift awkward things and work out why a pallet is damaged. That's what the pickers do, and I figure we'd be last to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the warehouse cut night staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask around. My cousin works at a depot across town, and the foreman there knows me. I'd move there, even on lower pay, if it kept me going until the degree is done. Family's how people find work round here.

say: I'd tell mates the warehouse will use **more machines**, but a patient still needs a person.
I'd say people should **keep learning** on the job.
think: The warehouse is where it bites first, so my **night shifts** could go.
I'd be left with a degree and **no income** to pay for it.
do: Ask my supervisor about the **stock control** desk, which checks deliveries.
Take **agency work** if my hours are cut, even without promises.
Spend only on **food and travel** until the exams are done.
feel: A bit **sick**, like hearing a storm is coming while still outside.
S1.quote: You can't automate a person carrying an old lady down the stairs.
fieldNote: Jamal's day job is the **exposed** part of his life; the paramedic degree is the secure part.
He relies on **family connections** for work, a practical not a political move.
Resistance to AI means he has no plan to use it, only to move around it.

steps.text: Ask the supervisor about the stock control desk
Spend only on food and travel until exams end
Ask my cousin about a job at the depot across town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too much, too quick, and nobody asked us. Two years is nothing. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, but I'd not post it online. I don't do that. I'd tell the lads to get a paper trail on what they're owed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be very worried. The warehouse job is gone within two years, I'd say, because ordering and planning is exactly what thinking AI does. Then my degree has two years left, and I'd be paying for it with no income. I've no savings to bridge that, and my mum can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the course office and ask what support there is for students who lose work. I'd look for any warehouse or delivery job that still needs a person, and I'd pick up every shift while they last. I'd tell my mum to sort out the bills. I wouldn't be learning anything new, I'd just try to hold on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted. Not panicking, I don't panic, but it sits in your chest like a stone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum and gran that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: Mum, Gran, it's going to be a bit tight, but I'll keep the degree going. I'd say we should look at what Gran's pension covers and what we can drop. I'd rather say it straight. They both worked all their lives and I'd not hide it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the gap before robots matter to a paramedic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters. Paramedics are hands-on, and the first robots that can do that are years away, and they'd need people next to them. So there's maybe a few more years there. But I'd be so broke by then that I might not make it to the job.

say: I'd say it's **too much, too quick**, and nobody asked us.
I'd tell the lads to keep a **paper trail** of what they're owed.
think: The warehouse job is **gone within two years**, because ordering and planning is what thinking AI does.
The degree has two years left and I'd have **no income** to pay for it.
do: Ask the course office what **support** exists for students who lose work.
Take **every shift** while the warehouse lasts.
Sit down with Mum and Gran and go through the **bills**.
feel: **Gutted**: it sits in my chest like a stone.
S2.quote: I'd be so broke by then that I might not make it to the job.
fieldNote: The short warning makes Jamal **alarmed**: he expects to lose his wage and has no savings.
His reaction is **practical and quiet**: bills, shifts, a straight talk with family.
He sees the 3-year robot gap for paramedics but fears running out of money before it helps.

steps.text: Take every warehouse shift while the job lasts
Ask the course office what support exists for students
Go through the bills with Mum and Gran

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it gives people a chance if they use it. I'd tell my mates to think about what jobs need people in the room, like care, repairs and emergency work. And I'd say the warehouse should be honest about what it plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be less scared. Five years is enough to finish the degree and get a job with the ambulance trust. The thinking AI would be around by 2031, but paramedics are hands-on and would last longer. I'd still worry about the three years before I qualify. Those are the dangerous ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and do the placements. I'd keep the warehouse job until it ends, then look for a care or ambulance support job on the side. I'd put money by every week, even a few pounds. I'd also try getting a driving licence for the ambulance trust, since they like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier. I can breathe a bit. Still not relaxed, I don't really do relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what I'm paying for. If a degree takes three years and I'm qualified at twenty-two with a job waiting, I'm a lot safer than if I'm still studying when the whole thing hits. Five years gets me over the line, just about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be your first move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the driving licence sorted. It's about eight hundred for lessons and the test. I'd do it off warehouse money. It's the one concrete thing that makes me more hireable, and it keeps me in front for emergency work.

say: I'd tell mates to think about jobs that **need people** in the room, like care and emergency work.
I'd say the warehouse should be **honest** about its plans.
think: Five years is enough to **finish the degree** and get an ambulance trust job.
The dangerous part is the **three years** before I qualify.
do: Pay about **eight hundred** for driving lessons and the test from warehouse money.
Put aside **a few pounds** every week.
feel: **Easier**, I can breathe a bit, though I don't really do relaxed.
S3.quote: If a degree takes three years and I'm qualified at twenty-two with a job waiting, I'm a lot safer than if I'm still studying when the whole thing hits.
fieldNote: Jamal's relief comes from **timing**: qualifying before the shock lands.
His one concrete plan is a **driving licence**, a typical practical, low-risk step.
He stays uneasy because the warehouse wage is exposed and money is tight until he qualifies.

steps.text: Pay for driving lessons and the test from warehouse money
Keep the warehouse job until it ends
Put aside a few pounds every week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and most of the worry is for people who ignore it. I'd say there's time for everyone to get ready, and nothing's going to fall on you overnight. I'd keep that to myself and the lads at work mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I'm fine. I'd qualify, work as a paramedic for a few years, and by 2036 I'd be an experienced one. Hands-on care is the last to go, around 2039. I'd feel safe in that picture. My mum and gran are the ones I'd still worry about, because their jobs and pensions are the exposed bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'm doing: degree, placements, a few years on the road. I'd pay off what I could of my loan and put some away for a deposit on a flat. I'd maybe try an AI tool at some point if the service started using it, because I'd have to. But I'd wait to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Steady. Almost boring, which I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do that you wouldn't do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about what the ambulance service wants from medics in 2030. If they use tablets and diagnosis tools, I'd learn them once they're proven. I don't try new things first. I wait for the lads to see if it works, then I do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your gran about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to worry. I'd say the world's changing, but I've got a trade that people always need. I'd say I'm looking out for her and Mum. She likes hearing that, and in this picture it's true.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty and worry is mostly for people who ignore it.
I'd tell my gran I have a **trade** people will always need.
think: I'd qualify and have **experience** by 2036, and hands-on care is the last to go.
My mum and gran are the **exposed** ones, through their jobs and pensions.
do: Do the **degree**, placements and a few years on the road.
Put money aside for a **flat deposit** and pay down some loan.
Try an AI tool only once the service uses it and it's **proven**.
S4.quote: I don't try new things first. I wait for the lads to see if it works, then I do it.
fieldNote: Jamal is **resistant** by nature: he adopts tools only after peers have, and only if required.
His worry shifts from himself to **his mum and gran**, whose work and pension are exposed.
With ten years he is steady, but money pressure keeps him uneasy rather than calm.

steps.text: Finish the degree and placements and work as a paramedic
Save for a flat deposit and pay down some loan
Wait to see if tablet tools work before learning them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time, no money, half a degree. What would help is somewhere that pays students on placements, a bit more bursary for people working nights, and honesty from the university about whether the ambulance service is still hiring. Real answers, not speeches.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Just that people like me don't shout about it. We get on and do the shifts. If someone wants to help, don't ask us to join a march. Fix the rent and the bursaries.

headlineQuote: People like me don't shout about it. We get on and do the shifts.
portrait: Jamal is a **19-year-old** paramedic science student who works night shifts at a warehouse and lives with his mum and gran.
He is a quiet, practical centrist who dislikes change and has **never used AI**.
His exposure is the **warehouse wage**: he knows ordering and routing go first, while paramedic work lasts longer.
He is anxious or alarmed when money is at risk and **uneasy** when time is on his side.
He relies on **family networks** and straight talk, not online posts or marches.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries him most, because he would be broke before the degree ends.
whatWouldHelp: Pay for students on **placements**, bursaries for night workers and honest word on whether ambulance jobs will exist.
